newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Labour says would not threaten Europe with vetoes.
newsitem.headline: Labour says would not threaten Europe with vetoes.

text.p: The man likely to negotiate for Britain at the inter-governmental conference (IGC) if the current government is defeated this spring said on Thursday a Labour administration would not threaten the bloc with vetoes.
Robin Cook, the opposition Labour Party's foreign policy spokesman, said his party wanted to bring Britain firmly back into the European fold.
"The most damage the Conservative government has done to our presence in Europe is that it has constantly adopted a negative position,...heckling on the sidelines of the game," Cook told reporters.
"I want to get (Britain) in the team," he said. The ruling Conservatives, he said, had sprayed around threats to veto the treaty unless it got its way.
The Labour Party is widely expected to win the British election, which could be held on May 1, leaving it to try to complete the IGC with its partners by a mid-June deadline in Amsterdam.
Cook, touted to be the foreign secretary in a Labour government, would lead Britain's negotiation team on the treaty.

He said Labour's stance would be sharply different from that of the Conservatives, including a lifting of threats to veto the negotiations if it did not get an array of things that London did not like. It would, he said:

-- Allow the Social Protocol to be brought into the treaty, ending Britain's opt-out and the Conservative threat to veto the whole treaty if it was not exempted from the Working Time directive (93/104/EC).
-- Support inclusion of an Employment Chapter in the treaty to make the fight against joblessness a formal priority.
-- Support adoption of language on environmental policies.
-- Support extending rights of protection to minorities and the disabled.

Cook also said Labour would consider calls for more Qualified Majority Voting on a case-by-case basis, accepting a loss of veto in some areas in exchange for a reweighting of votes in the Council of Ministers.
He said there could be no QMV in sensitive areas such as taxation and Common Foreign and Security Policy, but that QMV in the area of structural funding and some agriculture was possible.
With the EU set to enlarge, he said, it made sense to move away from unanimity in some areas.
"If we increase the European Union...are we really going to admit Cyprus, the Baltic States (and others) equipped with a veto?" he said.
"We are willing to consider on a case-by-case basis an extension of Qualified Majority Voting...(but) we would want to see that accompanied by a rewighting of votes," he said.
The flexibility on QMV is a sharp change from the Conservatives, who have made retention of the national veto a priority.
But Cook, who had earlier met European Commission President Jacques Santer, said Labour would retain Britain's border checks with other countries.

"We will retain external border controls because of the distinct geography of Britain," he said. "What may make sense for them (Britain's EU partners) does not make sense for an island nation," he said.
He said he believed a new treaty could be agreed by mid-June even though there would only be about six weeks between the election and the Amsterdam summit.
"I think I can do that," he said, adding that there was no particular need for a special summit as mooted by a number of EU officials.
He said a "round table" discussion after the election might be useful.
Labour had been well briefed on the negotiations by fellow Socialists, notably Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok.

"We are confident that we can show that a Labour government can do business with Europe in the interests of the British people in (contrast to) the way the Conservative government has failed," Cook said.
